service: CIPC — Companies and Intellectual Property Commission
overview: CIPC registers companies, co-operatives, and intellectual property (trademarks, patents, designs) in South Africa. If you want to start a formal business, you register it here. CIPC operates under the Companies Act 71 of 2008 and various intellectual property statutes.

company_types.description: The most common business structure in South Africa. Offers limited liability, meaning the directors and shareholders are generally not personally liable for company debts.
key_features: Minimum 1 director (must be a natural person, i.e. a real human)
Maximum 50 shareholders
Limited liability — shareholders only risk what they invested
Cannot offer shares to the public
Must file annual returns with CIPC
Separate legal entity from its owners
company_types.best_for: Most small and medium businesses, startups, freelancers wanting a formal structure, family businesses

company_types.description: Similar to a Pty Ltd, but directors are jointly and severally liable for debts and liabilities incurred during their period of office. Required by law for certain professions.
key_features: Directors are personally liable for company debts
Uses 'Incorporated' or 'Inc' as suffix
Required for regulated professions such as auditors, attorneys, accountants, engineers, and architects
Governed by the same rules as Pty Ltd companies, with the added personal liability provision
company_types.best_for: Professionals required by professional body rules — auditors, lawyers, accountants, engineers

company_types.description: A company formed for a public benefit purpose, cultural or social activity, communal or group interest. Cannot distribute profits or dividends to its members or incorporators.
key_features: Must have at least 3 directors
No shareholders — has members instead
All income must be used to advance the stated objectives
Cannot pay dividends or distribute profits to members
Can apply for tax exemption under Section 30 of the Income Tax Act
Can apply for PBO (Public Benefit Organisation) status with SARS
Must include 'NPC' as suffix in its name
company_types.best_for: NGOs, charities, community organisations, churches, sports clubs, professional associations

company_types.description: A foreign company that operates or has an office in South Africa. Must register with CIPC within 20 business days of beginning to conduct business in SA.
key_features: Must appoint a local representative in South Africa
Must maintain a registered office in South Africa
Subject to South African laws while operating here
Must file annual returns with CIPC
Registration fee: R175
company_types.best_for: Foreign companies expanding into the South African market

memorandum_of_incorporation.description: The MOI is the founding document of every company registered under the Companies Act. It sets out the rules governing the company's internal affairs.
memorandum_of_incorporation.standard_form: Use CIPC standard short form CoR15.1A for simple companies — this is a pre-approved template that covers the basics and is accepted without further review.
memorandum_of_incorporation.custom_moi: You can customise the MOI to suit your company's specific needs, but it must comply with the Companies Act 71 of 2008. A custom MOI should be prepared or reviewed by an attorney.
key_contents: Type of company (Pty Ltd, NPC, Inc, etc.)
Share structure — classes of shares, rights attached to each class, authorised number of shares
Quorum requirements for shareholders' and directors' meetings
Provisions for amending the MOI itself
Any special conditions or restrictions on the company's business
tips: For most simple Pty Ltd companies, the standard CoR15.1A is sufficient — do not overcomplicate things
If you have multiple shareholders, get a shareholders' agreement in addition to the MOI
Keep a signed copy of the MOI at the registered office at all times — this is a legal requirement
Amendments to the MOI require a special resolution (75% of shareholder votes)

services.name: Company Registration (Pty Ltd)
services.description: A private company (Proprietary Limited) is the most common business structure in South Africa. It provides limited liability protection to its shareholders.
requirements: At least one director who is a natural person (a real human, not another company)
A unique company name (check availability on the CIPC website)
A registered address in South Africa
A Memorandum of Incorporation (MOI) — CIPC provides a standard template (CoR15.1A)
Certified ID copies of all directors
Each director must have a valid South African ID number or passport (for foreign nationals)
how_to_register: Step 1: Create an account on www.cipc.co.za — you need a valid email address and SA ID or passport number
Step 2: Reserve your company name (R50) — takes 1-2 business days for approval. You can reserve up to 4 name options in one application
Step 3: Once the name is approved, complete the Notice of Incorporation (CoR14.1 form) — this includes company details, director information, and registered address
Step 4: Attach your MOI — use the CIPC standard short form CoR15.1A for a simple company, or upload a custom MOI prepared by an attorney
Step 5: Upload certified ID copies of all directors — the ID number must match exactly with Department of Home Affairs records
Step 6: Pay the registration fee of R175 online via credit/debit card or EFT
Step 7: CIPC issues a Registration Certificate and a B-BBEE Affidavit — usually within 1-5 business days
Step 8: Download your certificate and BEE affidavit from the CIPC portal under 'My Companies'
Step 9: Proceed immediately with post-registration steps (SARS, bank account, etc.)

costs.total: R225 for a basic Pty Ltd registration

after_registration: Register for tax with SARS (Income Tax, VAT if applicable, PAYE if you have employees)
Register for UIF if you have employees
Register for Compensation Fund (COIDA) if you have employees
Open a business bank account (you will need your registration certificate)
File annual returns with CIPC (due every year on your registration anniversary)

services.name: Annual Returns
services.description: Every registered company MUST file an annual return with CIPC every year. Failure to do so can result in your company being deregistered.
services.when: Due within 30 business days of your company's registration anniversary date each year. Check your exact due date on the CIPC website under 'Compliance Checklist'.
services.cost: R450 for a private company (Pty Ltd). R30 for a Close Corporation (CC).
how: Log in to the CIPC website
Navigate to 'Annual Returns'
Confirm or update your company details (registered address, director information, financial year end)
Confirm your company's financial statements status
Pay the fee online via credit/debit card or EFT
Receipt is issued immediately upon payment
what_happens_if_you_miss_it: Late filing results in a penalty fee added to the annual return cost
CIPC sends a compliance notice to the registered address
If you still don't file, CIPC begins the deregistration process
After 2 consecutive missed annual returns, the company will be deregistered
A deregistered company cannot trade, cannot enter contracts, and cannot sue or be sued
Bank accounts may be frozen when the bank discovers the deregistration
SARS may still hold directors personally liable for outstanding tax even after deregistration

services.name: Director Amendments
services.description: When you add, remove, or change directors of your company.
how: Log in to CIPC and submit a CoR39 form (change of directors)
Upload the new director's certified ID copy and signed consent letter (CoR39 consent)
The new director's ID must pass Department of Home Affairs verification
Fee: R50 per change
Processing: 1-3 business days
A director can resign by written notice to the company — the company must then file the CoR39 within 10 business days

services.name: Company Name Change
how: Reserve the new name (R50) — check availability first on the CIPC name search
Submit a special resolution signed by shareholders holding at least 75% of voting rights
Submit CoR9.4 form on the CIPC website
Fee: R175
Update your MOI to reflect the new name
Update your SARS registration with the new name
Update your business bank account details
Reprint any affected documents (letterheads, invoices, contracts)

services.name: Close Corporation (CC) Conversion
services.description: Close Corporations (CCs) can no longer be newly registered since 1 May 2011, but existing CCs can continue to operate or convert to Pty Ltd companies.
how: Submit a CK2A form to convert from CC to Pty Ltd
Prepare a new MOI for the company (CoR15.1A or custom)
Fee: R175
The CC registration number changes to a company registration number
You will need to update SARS records, bank accounts, and all contracts to reflect the new entity type and number
services.note: Existing CCs are still governed by the Close Corporations Act 69 of 1984, but the Companies Act increasingly applies. Conversion is recommended for long-term operation.

services.name: Trademark Registration
services.description: Protect your brand name, logo, or slogan from being used by others. Trademarks are classified under the Nice Classification system — you must register in each relevant class.
process: Step 1: Search existing trademarks at www.cipc.co.za (trademark search) to check if your desired mark is available or too similar to an existing one
Step 2: Identify the correct Nice Classification class(es) for your goods or services — there are 45 classes total (1-34 for goods, 35-45 for services)
Step 3: File a trademark application on the CIPC website or through a trademark attorney
Step 4: CIPC performs a formal examination of the application (takes 6-12 months due to backlogs)
Step 5: If approved, the trademark is published in the Patent Journal for a 3-month opposition window — any party can oppose during this period
Step 6: If no opposition (or opposition is unsuccessful), the trademark is registered
Step 7: Registration is valid for 10 years from the filing date, renewable for R400 per class
services.cost: R590 per class per trademark application
services.international_protection: South Africa is a member of the Madrid Protocol. You can extend your SA trademark internationally through a single application via WIPO (World Intellectual Property Organization). Additional fees apply per designated country.
tips: Consider using a trademark attorney for complex applications — errors can result in rejection and you lose the fee
A word mark protects the name regardless of font/style; a logo mark protects the specific visual design
Do a thorough search before applying — similar marks in the same class will be refused
You can use the TM symbol immediately upon filing; the registered symbol (R in a circle) only after registration is granted
Set a reminder to renew 6 months before the 10-year expiry

services.name: Patent Registration
services.description: Protect a new invention — a product, process, or method that is novel, involves an inventive step, and is capable of being used in industry.
process: Conduct a patent search to ensure your invention is novel
File a provisional patent application (gives you 12 months to file a complete application)
File a complete patent application with full specifications within 12 months of provisional filing
CIPC performs a formal examination (not a substantive search — SA uses a depository system)
Patent is granted if formalities are met
services.cost: R590 for application. Annual renewal fees apply to maintain the patent.
services.validity: 20 years from the filing date, subject to annual renewal fee payments
important_notes: South Africa uses a non-examining (depository) patent system — CIPC checks formalities only, not whether the invention is truly novel
This means invalid patents can be granted and may be challenged in court
Consider filing in multiple jurisdictions if your invention has international commercial value
Strongly recommended to use a patent attorney — patent specifications are highly technical legal documents

services.name: Design Registration
services.description: Protect the appearance of a product — either its aesthetic (how it looks) or functional (how it works) design.

types.description: Protects the visual appearance — shape, pattern, ornamentation, or configuration of an article
Protects a design dictated by the function the article performs

services.note: Designs must be new and not previously disclosed to the public before filing.

services.name: Copyright
services.description: Protection for original literary, musical, artistic works, films, sound recordings, broadcasts, published editions, and computer programs.
key_facts: Copyright is automatic in South Africa — no registration is required
Protection begins the moment the work is created in a material form (written down, recorded, etc.)
There is no copyright registration office in South Africa
Copyright lasts for 50 years after the death of the author (for literary, musical, and artistic works)
Keep dated records of your work creation process as evidence of ownership
Copyright infringement can be pursued through the courts

services.name: Deregistration and Re-instatement
services.description: Companies that fail to comply with CIPC requirements can be deregistered. Deregistered companies can apply to be re-instated.
deregistration: A company is deregistered after 2 consecutive missed annual returns
CIPC may also deregister a company if it has reason to believe the company is not carrying on business
Once deregistered, the company ceases to exist as a legal entity
The company cannot trade, enter into contracts, open bank accounts, or sue or be sued
Directors may face personal liability for debts incurred after deregistration
re_instatement: Submit a CoR40.5 application on the CIPC website
Pay the re-instatement fee of R700
File and pay all outstanding annual returns (approximately R450 each for a Pty Ltd)
Pay any penalty fees for late filing
Provide a reason why the company should be re-instated
Processing takes 2-4 weeks once all documents and payments are submitted
The company retains its original registration number upon re-instatement

post_registration_checklist.description: After registering your company with CIPC, you must complete several additional steps before you can fully operate.

details: Company Income Tax (CIT) — mandatory for all companies, register within 60 days of incorporation
Pay As You Earn (PAYE) — required if you have employees or directors earning a salary
Value Added Tax (VAT) — mandatory if annual turnover exceeds R1 million; voluntary registration allowed if turnover exceeds R50,000
Skills Development Levy (SDL) — required if annual payroll exceeds R500,000
Register via SARS eFiling (www.sarsefiling.co.za) or visit a SARS branch

Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF) — mandatory if you have any employees. Contribution: 2% of salary (1% employer, 1% employee). Register at your nearest Department of Employment and Labour office or via uFiling (www.ufiling.co.za)

Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act (COIDA) — mandatory if you have any employees. Protects employees injured at work. Register at the Compensation Fund (www.labour.gov.za). Annual assessment fee varies by industry risk category

Required documents: CIPC Registration Certificate, Memorandum of Incorporation (MOI), certified ID copies of all directors, proof of business address (utility bill or lease agreement), company resolution authorising account opening
All major banks (FNB, Standard Bank, Nedbank, Absa, Capitec Business) offer business accounts
Compare fees — monthly charges range from R0 (digital-only) to R500+ depending on the bank and account type
Some banks offer free or discounted banking for the first year for new businesses
Digital banks like TymeBank Business and Bank Zero have lower fees but fewer physical services

steps.step: Register on the Central Supplier Database (CSD)
details: Required if you want to do business with any government department, municipality, or state-owned entity
Register at www.csd.gov.za — it is free
You need: company registration certificate, tax clearance, bank account details, B-BBEE certificate or affidavit, director details
Registration is verified against CIPC, SARS, and bank records — ensure all details match exactly
CSD registration is valid for a set period and must be kept up to date
CIDB (Construction Industry Development Board) — if you are in the construction industry
Tourism grading — if you are in hospitality, apply via the Tourism Grading Council
Sector-specific licences — liquor licence, health permits for food businesses, environmental authorisations
Municipal business licence — check with your local municipality for requirements

bbbee.title: Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (B-BBEE)
bbbee.description: B-BBEE is a South African government policy aimed at redressing economic inequality. Your B-BBEE level affects your ability to win government contracts and do business with large corporates.

levels.turnover: Less than R10 million per year
levels.level: Automatic Level 4 (or Level 1 if 51%+ black-owned, Level 2 if 100% black-owned)
levels.requirements: No verification needed. Obtain a sworn affidavit from a Commissioner of Oaths confirming turnover and ownership. CIPC issues a B-BBEE affidavit with your registration certificate.
levels.cost: Free (affidavit from Commissioner of Oaths) or included in CIPC registration

levels.turnover: R10 million to R50 million per year
levels.level: Depends on scorecard — must be verified
levels.requirements: Must obtain a B-BBEE certificate from an accredited verification agency (SANAS-accredited). Measured on all 5 elements of the scorecard: ownership, management control, skills development, enterprise and supplier development, socio-economic development.
levels.cost: R3,000 to R8,000 for verification, depending on the agency

levels.turnover: More than R50 million per year
levels.level: Depends on full scorecard — must be verified
levels.requirements: Full verification by a SANAS-accredited B-BBEE verification agency. Measured on all 5 elements with stricter targets.
levels.cost: R8,000 to R15,000+ for verification, depending on complexity

tips: Keep your B-BBEE affidavit or certificate up to date — many tenders require it
If you are an EME, a simple sworn affidavit is all you need — do not pay a verification agency for this
Sector-specific codes (e.g., construction, ICT, tourism) may have different thresholds and targets
B-BBEE certificates are typically valid for 12 months

director_responsibilities.description: Company directors in South Africa have significant legal responsibilities under the Companies Act 71 of 2008.

duties.details: Directors must act in good faith, in the best interest of the company, and for a proper purpose. They must not use their position or company information for personal gain.

duties.duty: Duty of Care, Skill, and Diligence (Section 76)
duties.details: Directors must exercise the degree of care, skill, and diligence that may reasonably be expected of a person carrying out the same functions and having the same knowledge and experience.
Directors must declare any personal financial interest in a matter before the board. They must recuse themselves from voting on matters where they have a conflict.

duties.duty: Not Trade While Insolvent (Section 22 and Section 77)
duties.details: Directors are personally liable if the company continues to trade when it is reasonably foreseeable that the company cannot pay its debts as they fall due. This is known as reckless trading.

disqualification: A person is disqualified from being a director if they are under 18, declared mentally unfit by a court, or an unrehabilitated insolvent
A court can declare a director delinquent under Section 162 for gross abuse of position, fraud, or persistent non-compliance with the Companies Act
A delinquent director is prohibited from serving as a director for a period determined by the court (minimum 7 years)
CIPC maintains a register of disqualified directors — this is checked during company registration
personal_liability_risks: Trading while insolvent — directors are jointly and severally liable for company debts
Signing contracts on behalf of a deregistered company — directors are personally liable
Failure to pay SARS — directors can be held personally liable for outstanding company taxes
Fraud or misrepresentation — criminal charges and personal liability

company_secretary.description: A company secretary is responsible for ensuring the company complies with the Companies Act and its MOI.
requirements: Not required for private companies (Pty Ltd) with only 1 director
Required if the company has a board of directors (2+ directors) — though many small Pty Ltd companies overlook this requirement in practice
Required for public companies and state-owned companies
The company secretary can be a natural person or a company/firm
Must have the requisite knowledge of, or experience in, relevant laws and corporate governance
duties: Ensure CIPC filings (annual returns, director changes, etc.) are submitted on time
Maintain company records and minute books
Advise directors on their duties and responsibilities
Ensure shareholder meetings are properly convened and conducted

cipc_offices.name: CIPC Head Office — Pretoria
cipc_offices.address: the dti Campus, Block F, 77 Meintjies Street, Sunnyside, Pretoria
cipc_offices.note: Head office handles complex matters and escalations. Most services are online.

cipc_offices.name: CIPC Self-Service Terminal — Durban
cipc_offices.address: 267 Anton Lembede Street, Durban CBD (at the Department of Employment and Labour)
cipc_offices.note: Limited services available in person — most CIPC services are online only

cipc_offices.name: CIPC Self-Service Terminal — Cape Town
cipc_offices.address: 22 Long Street, Cape Town CBD (at the Department of Employment and Labour)
cipc_offices.note: Self-service terminals for basic CIPC transactions

online_portal.services: Company registration, annual returns, director changes, trademark applications, name reservations, company searches, certificate downloads, B-BBEE affidavits
tips: Use Chrome or Microsoft Edge browser — other browsers may cause issues
Clear your browser cache and cookies if pages don't load or you see errors
Best times to use the website: Monday to Thursday, 6:00 AM - 8:00 AM — the site is much faster during off-peak hours
Screenshot every step of your application — if something goes wrong, you have evidence
Save your reference numbers immediately — you will need them for any follow-up
Customer query queue system: book a callback or in-person appointment at www.cipc.co.za under 'Customer Query'
For payment issues, always use the exact reference number provided — do not modify it
EFT payments can take 24-48 hours to reflect on the CIPC system

important_contacts.physical_office: the dti Campus, Block F, 77 Meintjies Street, Sunnyside, Pretoria

common_problems.problem: CIPC website not working / constantly timing out
common_problems.what_to_do: This is a very common complaint. Use Chrome or Edge browser. Clear cache and cookies. Try early morning between 6:00 AM and 8:00 AM on weekdays. If persistent, call 086 100 2472. CIPC has acknowledged ongoing website performance issues. Screenshot error messages for your records.

Try variations of your desired name — add a geographic qualifier (e.g., 'KZN', 'Durban'), change the word order, or use a creative spelling. You can submit up to 4 name options in one reservation. Avoid generic or descriptive names as they are more likely to clash. Use the CIPC name search tool to check before paying the reservation fee.

common_problems.problem: Director ID not verified / verification failed
common_problems.what_to_do: The director's ID number and personal details must match exactly with Department of Home Affairs records. Check for typos in the ID number. Ensure the name used matches the ID document exactly (including middle names if on the ID). If the director recently changed their name or has a new ID, it may take time to update in the system. Foreign nationals must use their passport number and may need to verify at a CIPC office.

EFT payments take 24-48 hours to reflect. Use the exact reference number provided — do not add spaces or change any characters. If payment does not reflect after 48 hours, email proof of payment to info@cipc.co.za with your application reference number. Keep your bank proof of payment as evidence.

Try again during early morning hours (6:00 AM - 8:00 AM). Screenshot every page before clicking 'Next' or 'Submit'. If the application was partially submitted, log in later and check 'My Applications' — it may have been saved. Do not re-submit and pay twice without first checking.

common_problems.problem: Company deregistered for not filing annual returns
common_problems.what_to_do: Apply for re-instatement on the CIPC website. Submit a CoR40.5 form. Fee: R700 plus all outstanding annual returns (approximately R450 each for Pty Ltd) plus penalty fees. Processing takes 2-4 weeks. You will need to provide a reason for the re-instatement.

common_problems.problem: Someone registered a company using your identity
common_problems.what_to_do: Report immediately to CIPC and to SAPS (South African Police Service). CIPC will investigate and can deregister the fraudulent company. Check your credit report for any business accounts opened in your name. File a complaint with the Information Regulator if your personal information was misused.

Download it from the CIPC website — log in and navigate to 'My Companies'. If it is not there, check under 'My Applications' for status. If the application is approved but the certificate is not showing, call 086 100 2472 with your reference number.

scams_and_fraud_warnings.description: There are numerous scams targeting business owners that impersonate CIPC or claim to offer CIPC services. Be vigilant.

common_scams.details: Letters or emails demanding payment for 'compliance certificates', 'annual compliance fees', or 'company verification'. These are NOT from CIPC. CIPC does not send letters demanding immediate payment via third parties.

Websites that look similar to the official CIPC site but charge 5-10 times the official fee. They may or may not actually process your registration. The only official website is www.cipc.co.za — do not use any other site for CIPC services.

SMS or email messages claiming your annual return is overdue and providing a link to pay. These links lead to fraudulent payment portals. Always go directly to www.cipc.co.za to check and file your annual return.

common_scams.scam: Third parties claiming to be CIPC agents
common_scams.details: People visiting businesses in person claiming to be CIPC inspectors or agents demanding fees. CIPC does not send inspectors to demand payments at your premises.

how_to_protect_yourself: Only use the official CIPC website: www.cipc.co.za
Never pay CIPC fees to a third party or via a link in an email/SMS
Verify any communication by calling CIPC directly: 086 100 2472
Report suspected scams to CIPC and to the SAPS
Check the CIPC website for official fee schedules — if someone charges significantly more, it is likely a scam

escalation.step_2: Book a query via the CIPC customer query system at www.cipc.co.za
escalation.step_3: Email a formal complaint to info@cipc.co.za with all reference numbers, screenshots, and a clear description of the issue
escalation.step_4: Escalate to the CIPC Commissioner's office if no response within 10 business days
escalation.step_5: Lodge a complaint with the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC) — www.thedtic.gov.za
escalation.step_6: As a last resort, approach the Companies Tribunal for disputes related to CIPC decisions
escalation.legislation: Companies Act 71 of 2008, Close Corporations Act 69 of 1984, Trade Marks Act 194 of 1993, Patents Act 57 of 1978, Designs Act 195 of 1993, Copyright Act 98 of 1978

your_rights: You have the right to register a company if you meet the requirements — CIPC cannot unreasonably refuse
CIPC must process applications within the published timeframes
You have the right to access the public company register — anyone can search for company information
Your personal information held by CIPC is protected under POPIA (Protection of Personal Information Act)
You have the right to appeal CIPC decisions to the Companies Tribunal
You have the right to a refund if CIPC fails to deliver a paid service (submit a written request)
Trademark applicants have the right to respond to any objections raised during the examination process
